intelligence.human_view: Too glowy is not glowing — it is a wash, and a wash covers the object the way the underglow law already forbids: light over the object instead of light with volume around it. The weekdays are objects — each day a ball, a jewel, a real thing — and a real thing does not disappear into its own glow. A diamond that disappears is not a diamond: it is a picture that failed to be an object, and a picture that disappears is worse than no diamond at all. The rule he gives is the escape hatch, not a surrender: if the diamond can't be made real, do something that CAN be made real — a spinning ball, a clock, a gauge. Real is the requirement; the shape is the choice. Just enough glow — the standing law — and the object itself, sharp and touchable, underneath it.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine a beautiful shiny marble, and someone shines such a bright torch on it that you can't even see the marble anymore — just bright light everywhere! That's too glowy. And imagine a little diamond in the corner that just... disappears, like it was never there. That's not a real diamond! Shawn says: turn the glow down so you can see the real thing, and if the diamond can't look real, make something else instead — a spinning ball, or a clock, or a gauge. It has to look real!
intelligence.grandma_view: Dear, Shawn says Sunday, Monday, Tuesday are glowing far too much, dear — they don't look like real objects anymore, just bright light. Turn the glow down, dear, and make them look lovely and real. And the little diamonds in the corner, dear — they don't look real at all, they just disappear! If a diamond can't be made to look real, dear, make something that can — a spinning ball, or a clock, or a gauge. It has to look real, dear.
intelligence.naya_view: WEEKDAY GLOW + THE DIAMOND. TONE THE GLOW DOWN — REAL LIKE REAL OBJECTS. A DIAMOND THAT DISAPPEARS IS NOT A DIAMOND. IF IT CAN'T BE MADE REAL, MAKE SOMETHING THAT CAN: A SPINNING BALL, A CLOCK, A GAUGE. IT HAS TO LOOK REAL.
